notes: *ḱred dʰeh₁- 'put trust (in someone)', with the one trusted in the dative (Schmitt 1967 §§445–449, after Darmesteter and Köhler; de Vaan 2008 s.v. crēdō): Indo-Iranian (Ved. śrad-dhā-, often in tmesis śrát … dhā-; Av. zrazdā-), Italic (Lat. crēdō) and Celtic (OIr. creitid). Parallels, all checked locally: RV 2.12.5 śrát asmai dhatta 'put trust in him!' (2pl imperative + dative of the anaphoric pronoun, of Indra; vedaweb); Plaut. Epid. 340 crede modo mihi 'just believe me' (2sg imperative + dative; LASLA); Wb. 18c11 ni cretid dó (Doyle's Würzburg glosses, tagged creitid; of an angel preaching another gospel). With ní this is the 2pl present indicative, 'you do not believe him'; the Thesaurus's 'believe him not' renders the sense. So the Irish shares the 2pl and the dative of the one trusted (do 'to him'), not the imperative mood. Support: RV 1.103.5 śrát índrasya dhattana vīryā̀ya 'put trust in Indra's heroism' (2pl imperative + dative; vedaweb), Catull. 12.6 crede Pollioni (LASLA), and Avestan (same branch as Vedic): OAv. Y. 31.1 yōi zrazdā̊ aŋhən mazdāi 'who will be trusting in Mazdā' (the adjective, with the dative), and the YAv. tmesis zrasca dāt̰ (Yt. 9.26 per Schmitt §446 = CAB YtDru7.4j; also YtAshi9.4g), both checked in CAB. The line follows the Vedic: 2pl imperative, 3sg dative. Latin has the 2sg imperative, Old Irish the negated 2pl indicative; neither the Latin number nor the Irish mood and negation is in the line. Secure: the verb, exact in all three branches. Formation: the engine's lexeme is the unreduplicated athematic ḱréddʰeh₁- (the handbook lemma). Vedic has the reduplicated present (dádhāti; dhatta is its weak 2pl), Latin and Celtic a thematized *ḱred-dʰh₁-e/o- (de Vaan). So the zero-grade *dʰh₁- of the 2pl ḱreddʰh₁té is what all three presuppose, but the present stem agrees only at root level. The Vedic tmesis is not modelled: the engine writes the univerbated verb. Interpolated: the dative pronoun (Ved. asmai, Lat. mihi, OIr. dó are different pronouns). The engine's primary h₁ésmey has *-ey, while Ved. asmai points to *h₁ésmōy, which the engine lists as the alternative form.

plan.english: You are the god of the gods.

notes: 'God of gods', the elative figure of a noun with its own genitive plural (West 2007 ch. 2, citing TB 2.6.8.3 devānāṃ devam and the Carmen Saliare diuom deo supplicate 'pray to the god of gods'). In Vedic it is a formula: deváḥ devā́nām in RV 1.31.1, 1.68.2, 1.94.13, 9.95.2, 9.97.7, 10.48.11, 10.150.4 (vedaweb, all checked). Latin: diuom deo in the Salian hymn quoted by Varro, L.L. 7.27 (Baehrens, FPR p. 29, fr. 1.2; checked in the local OCR with its apparatus). Both words continue *deywós in both branches: Lat. deus and dīuus both go back to *deiwos, and diuom is the old gen. pl. in -om. Manuscript: the Florentinus reads diuum (Baehrens prints diuom) deo supplicante. supplicate is Grotefend's correction, so only the noun phrase is cited. Case: the Vedic is a predicate nominative with the copula (RV 1.94.13 deváḥ devā́nām asi 'you are the god of gods', of Agni; RV 1.31.1 with abhavaḥ 'you became'). The Latin is a dative object. The line follows the Vedic. The same stanza RV 1.94.13 has the parallel vásur vásūnām 'the good one of the good ones', which shows the figure is productive in Vedic (evidence for the figure, not for the lexeme). Word order: the engine puts the genitive first (deywṓm deywós), as in the Latin diuom deo; the Vedic has the head first. Secure: *deywós, both head and genitive. Interpolated: the copula h₁ési and the 2nd person (Vedic asi; the Latin has no copula). Limits: the figure type is widespread (West lists Greek, Latin and Norse examples built on other words), so the claim is for this lexical realization in two branches, not for the figure. The Carmen Saliare is a fragmentary, partly unintelligible text.

'The immortal gods'. West 2007 ch. 3: Vedic devā́ amṛ́tāḥ (RV 3.4.11 etc.); 'In Latin, the expected *immortus is replaced by the extended form immortalis. The gods are the di immortales'. Phase 8c accepted claim C046. Parallels, both with the noun phrase as the accusative object of a verb of addressing the gods: RV 10.65.15 (= 10.66.15) devā́n vásiṣṭho amṛ́tān vavande 'Vasiṣṭha has praised the immortal gods' (vedaweb), and Plaut. Amph. 1093 inuocat deos inmortalis 'she calls on the immortal gods' (LASLA). Support: RV 3.4.11 devā́ amṛ́tāḥ (vedaweb) and Cato, Orig. 4 fr. 7 dii immortales (LASLA), both nominative. Secure: *deywós (Ved. devá-, Lat. deus), exact. *n̥mr̥tós is exact only in Vedic (amṛ́ta-). Lat. in-mortālis has the same privative and root but a different formation, the privative of the -āli- derivative of mors (*mr̥-ti-), as West says: root level only, and the builder finds no Latin path for it at all, so it is not claimed as secure. Revised after round 4: cut to the NP, as an np utterance in the accusative (r4: the interpolated verb ǵʰuHéyeti made the frame larger than the core). The verbs are not cognate (Ved. vand- 'praise', Lat. in-uocāre 'call on'), so no verb is shared. Case: accusative plural in both parallels (RV 10.65.15 devā́n … amŕ̥tān, VedaWeb ACC PL, object of vavande; Plaut. Amph. 1093 deos inmortalis, LASLA Case=Acc, object of inuocat). Caveat: Plautus adapts a Greek original, so di immortales there may render ἀθάνατοι θεοί. Limit: 'immortal' as the standing epithet of the gods is a near-universal pairing. The claim rests on the Vedic–Greek formula with *n̥mr̥tós, with Latin as a renewed reflex, so this is a weak line.

Round 3 draft (docs/audits/tier2-round3-drafts.md), from the formula witness scan (docs/research/formula-witness-scan.md); not yet reviewed. West 2007 ch. 3 'race of gods' (west_ch03_f07). Vedic devā́nāṃ jánma 'the race of the gods', checked in VedaWeb: RV 6.51.2b, RV 1.70.6b (devā́nāṃ jánma mártāṃś ca vidvā́n 'knowing the race of the gods and the mortals'); also 6.51.12d, and jánimāni at 4.27.1b, 7.42.2b, 9.83.4b. Latin (index unit text, Perseus Latin): Catull. 64.23 heroes, salvete, deum genus (vocative apposition), Lucr. 5.1156 divom genus humanumque. *deywós is exact in both (devá-, deus/divus). The head *ǵénh₁os 'race' is exact in Latin (genus) and root level in Vedic (jánman-, *ǵénh₁mn̥; Ved. jánas- occurs once in the RV and not in this phrase). The lexeme *ǵénh₁mn̥ would be exact for Vedic but is glossed 'offspring, seed', so the line uses *ǵénh₁os ('race, lineage'). Greek γένος (= genus) with renewed θεῶν (Hes. Th. 21 ἀθανάτων ἱερὸν γένος) is not cited. Case: nominative (Vedic accusative, Latin vocative and accusative).
